content.overview: A contingent contract is a contract to do or not to do something if some event collateral to the contract does or does not happen. Enforcement depends on the event under ss. 32–36.

sections.heading: Structure
sections.body: Identify the collateral event. Contingent contracts cannot be enforced until the event happens (s. 32); if the event becomes impossible, the contract becomes void.

sections.heading: Track B
sections.body: Plead the contingency and its occurrence or failure. Distinguish conditions precedent from ordinary promises.

illustrations: A promises to pay B a sum if B’s house is destroyed by fire. The obligation depends on the collateral event; enforcement follows the contingency rules when the specified event occurs.

enhancement.detailedExplanation:
Statutory rule: Sections 31–36 define contingent contracts and prescribe when they may be enforced or become void depending on the happening, non-happening or impossibility of the collateral event on which the contract depends.

Definition: A contingent contract is a contract to do or not to do something if some event, collateral to the contract, happens or does not happen.

Ingredients / conditions:
1. There must be a valid underlying contract.
2. Performance must depend on an uncertain future event collateral to the contract.
3. Apply the relevant rule for an event happening, not happening, becoming impossible, or falling within the fixed-time rules.
4. Enforcement follows the statutory timing and impossibility conditions in sections 32–36.
examples: A promises to pay B a sum if B’s house is destroyed by fire. The obligation depends on the collateral event; enforcement follows the contingency rules when the specified event occurs.

distinctions: Contingent contract vs absolute contract: a contingent contract depends on the happening or non-happening of a collateral uncertain event; an absolute contract is not conditioned in that manner.
Contingent contract vs wagering agreement: the statutory requirements and legal consequences differ; the facts must be tested against the relevant provisions rather than labels alone.
